algorithms.name: Building, checking and landing one batch
steps: Start when the project has no batch running and the oldest queued landing has waited BATCH_GATHER_SECONDS (60). Take up to MAX_BATCH (8) queued landings in approval order, moving each prerequisite ahead of its dependents and leaving out a task whose prerequisite is neither landed nor taken.

Read main's tip T. Build the chain: base = T; for each task, merge each frozen target onto base with merge-tree and commit-tree (Hub identity, message 'Integrate approved work <sha12>'). A task that does not merge cleanly is taken out and sent back with its paths; otherwise its last commit is prefix P_k.

If the full chain's tree has passed every configured check before, record the pass; otherwise run the checks on the last prefix in a scratch worktree, stopping at the first failure that is the batch's own.

On a failure, re-run the failed tests on the same tree. A pass there records the flake and counts as a pass. Then run the failed tests on T: if every confirmed failure fails there too, apply slice M's decision and stop.

On a confirmed failure of the batch's own: binary-search k over the prefixes, running the failed tests (or the failing check) on P_k, to find the smallest failing k. Send task k back. Land P_(k-1) only if the tasks before k already had a full pass on exactly P_(k-1)'s tree; otherwise re-queue tasks 1..k-1 and k+1..n at the head as the next batch.

On a pass: under the mutation lock and with no transaction open, fast-forward main from T to the checked prefix (git merge --ff-only). If main is no longer at T, mark the batch superseded and go back to the first step.
In one short transaction, record the batch landed and one integration row per target for each landed task. After commit, broadcast, run refresh and re-drain queued turns.

design:
D1. Integration is specified apart from the transition machine: the merge and the status map are tested and fail differently. Gates that refuse approval because of what would be merged live here; gates about who may approve stay in task-lifecycle-governance.

D2. Approval means integration. Approving merges, locally and in the same operation, the commits accepted evidence names (reduced by ancestry per line of work), or the task's own branch tip where evidence does not govern; never an agent branch, never a remote.

D3. Integration never rolls back the approval. Preconditions that make it impossible are recorded skips; a failed merge is aborted and recorded. Each attempt is an append-only `task_integrations` row with outcome, reason, riders, mechanism `local`, and `retryable` decided by `task_integration.is_retryable`.

D4. Gates that ask "what would merge" (conflict, unaccepted evidence) run only when `merge_situation` resolves (main branch set and existing, workspace resolvable, a repository). The live-turn refusal is not about the repository and applies everywhere. A git call that raises is a refusal (`GitUnavailableError`), not a 500 and not an approval.

D5. The preview asks the same `merge_situation` and test merge as the gate, so the two cannot disagree, but it never refuses and moves nothing.
lifecycle: Split out of task-lifecycle-governance in the 2026-10-08 spec overhaul.
problem: Approval is the moment work reaches the main line. If it merges the wrong commit, merges over a conflict, or quietly records nothing, an approved task does not mean the code is in.

requirements.rationale: Approval is what places work in the product; a terminal state with no such meaning cannot answer whether anything approved shipped. Naming commits rather than branches narrows what lands to the approved work; per-task branches make the ancestry match the task, and riders are recorded where it does not.
requirements.statement: The move into `approved` SHALL record the verdict at once and queue the task's work for landing on the project's configured main branch, its merge targets frozen at that moment. Without checks configured the landing SHALL run right after the approval and the approval SHALL answer with its outcome; with checks configured it SHALL land in a batch once the batch's checks pass. Where evidence governs the task, what lands SHALL be the commits named by its accepted evidence footprints, reduced per line of work so that a commit another kept commit contains is dropped; evidence awaiting review or rejected SHALL contribute nothing. A landing to main SHALL be local: it SHALL NOT contact a remote, push, or need a credential (a build that lands as a pull request is the one case that pushes, see Pull request landing), and SHALL record the commits that rode along with each merge.

requirements.rationale: A conflict found mid-merge would leave a task recorded approved and a repository half-changed. The two remedies differ because re-approving re-judges a branch tip but not a commit evidence names (F155). A reviewer is not the one to resolve the author's conflict (F504).
requirements.statement: The Hub SHALL refuse a move to `approved` when a commit approval would merge conflicts with the main branch, tested by a merge that touches neither working tree nor index, at every rigor. The refusal SHALL name the conflicting paths, the judged commit and the branch it was recorded on (distinct from the target branch), say when another task recorded that evidence, say when the commit is no longer on that branch (and nothing when that cannot be determined), and state the remedy for its source: for a commit named by accepted evidence, resolve on that branch, record evidence from a checkout of that branch and have it accepted (the operator's unless an agent is granted it); for a task's own branch tip, resolve on the branch and approve again. It SHALL end by telling a reviewer to send the task back with `revision_needed`.

requirements.rationale: Approval is a judgement that the work is good; a repository condition is not a reason to reverse it, and coverage then says `verified, not integrated`. The Hub writes documents into the project, so its own writes must not block the document's own task merges (F515).
requirements.statement: The move into `approved` SHALL still succeed, with the integration recorded as skipped and its reason, when the project has no main branch (or none by the configured name), its workspace cannot be resolved, it is not a repository, the checkout has uncommitted changes to tracked files, the checkout is on another branch, nothing accepted names a commit where evidence governs, or the task has no branch of its own where it does not. Untracked files, and tracked document files whose content is exactly what the Hub last wrote, SHALL NOT count as uncommitted changes. A merge that fails SHALL be aborted and recorded as `failed` without rolling back the approval.

requirements.rationale: The account of what the Hub wrote into the operator's repository must not be editable by the thing that wrote it, and the mechanism keeps a future integration mode distinguishable.
requirements.statement: The Hub SHALL record every integration attempt with the task, commit, source and target branches, outcome (`merged`, `skipped` or `failed`), reason, the commits that rode along, the mechanism (`local`), the actor and the time, and SHALL offer no route that edits or removes one; a record goes only when its task is deleted.

requirements.rationale: A merge of an ancestor succeeds and changes nothing; recording it as merged makes a no-op look like work reaching the product. An operator mid-edit deserves the true reason.
requirements.statement: Where the commit to integrate is already reachable from the main branch, the Hub SHALL record the attempt as skipped with that reason, not as merged, and SHALL decide this before checking the working tree.

requirements.rationale: Restating `approved` is a no-op, so without a retry the remedy a skip asks for does nothing. The classification lives with the reasons, so the app never derives behaviour from a sentence, and an unclassified reason gets no button by default.
requirements.statement: The Hub SHALL let the operator and agents retry integration for an approved task, refusing (HTTP 409) a task that is not approved, and SHALL mark each recorded attempt `retryable` when a retry could change it: a failed merge, a dirty checkout, a checkout on another branch, or an unavailable workspace. No main branch, not a repository, nothing to merge, no task branch and already-integrated SHALL NOT be offered a retry. A retry requested directly SHALL be attempted and recorded whatever the last reason was.

requirements.rationale: The skip told the operator to choose a branch; discharging that at the moment they do makes the instruction true. Other skip reasons are not changed by naming a branch.
requirements.statement: Saving a project's main branch SHALL attempt integration again for each approved task whose most recent attempt was skipped for want of one, and only those; the setting SHALL save even if an attempt fails.

requirements.rationale: A task's own branch carries only its work; an agent's branch carries every task the agent touched, and merging it is a defect already recorded at the highest severity. A flow, or a task linked to a requirement, has not asked to stop being governed by its requirements, and only evidence can carry another task's commit on a shared requirement.
requirements.statement: Where evidence does not govern a task (its loop declared its work needs no evidence, or it is on a loop with no document and links no requirement), approval SHALL merge the commit at the tip of the task's own branch, tested for conflicts first like an evidence commit; with no branch of its own nothing SHALL merge and the reason SHALL say so. Evidence governs a task with no loop, on a loop whose id does not resolve, on a loop that declared it needs evidence, on a flow (a loop with a document) that made no declaration, or that links a requirement.

requirements.rationale: The unaccepted-evidence refusal tells the reader to accept; doing so must land the work, including the mixed case where approval already merged other accepted evidence. Whether the commit is in main is asked of the repository, so a commit already there is recorded as already integrated.
requirements.statement: Accepting evidence that names a commit SHALL attempt integration for every approved task linked to that evidence's requirement that has not already recorded a merge of that commit, attributed to whoever accepted it, recording a skip where the repository cannot take it; rejecting evidence SHALL attempt nothing, and the acceptance SHALL stand even if the attempt fails.

requirements.rationale: The refusal is otherwise the only place a conflict is stated, and it cannot be read before the first approval or after it. Asking the same question as the gate keeps the two from disagreeing.
requirements.statement: The integration preview (`GET /tasks/{id}/integration-preview`) SHALL say what approval would merge and whether it merges cleanly, using the same test merge as the approval refusal, naming conflicting paths and commit when it does not; it SHALL move no branch, change no working tree or index, record nothing, and be computed on request. It SHALL not claim a clean merge when approval would merge nothing, SHALL state the real commit count, SHALL say the merge is checked at approval where the Hub cannot ask (no main branch, workspace, repository or configured branch), and SHALL answer successfully, saying git could not be asked, when a git call fails.

requirements.rationale: Otherwise accepting a sibling's evidence merged it through another approved task, bypassing the sibling's own review and checks (F520).
requirements.statement: Evidence recorded by a different task SHALL count toward a task's merge targets, and toward its unaccepted-evidence refusal, only once that recording task is `approved`; evidence recorded by the task itself or by no task SHALL count as before.

requirements.rationale: Until the turn ends its edits are uncommitted, so whatever approval would merge contains none of the work (F162). A reviewer approving from inside its own bound turn must not be refused by itself. A dead process with a stale status must not block approval forever.
requirements.statement: The Hub SHALL refuse a move to `approved` while a run bound to the task, other than the run requesting the move, has a live process, naming the agent whose turn is running and stating that the refusal clears itself when the turn ends. Liveness SHALL be tested on the process, not the recorded run status. The refusal SHALL apply at every rigor and whether or not the project can integrate.

requirements.rationale: Approving there records the work as good and merges nothing while a commit waits unjudged. A task with no evidence (research, decisions) stays approvable. A commit already in main through another task does not count as new (F499); an unknown counts as new so it never refuses.
requirements.statement: The Hub SHALL refuse a move to `approved` where evidence for the task naming a commit is awaiting review and nothing approval would merge is new to the main branch. Each waiting piece SHALL be named with the task that recorded it, and the refusal SHALL name both remedies (accept it, or grant an agent the capability to accept it). Rejected evidence and evidence naming no commit SHALL NOT cause it, and it SHALL NOT fire where integration could not be attempted (no main branch, unresolvable workspace, not a repository, or no branch by the configured name). Where something new would merge, the waiting evidence SHALL be reported on the approval instead.

requirements.rationale: The gate exists so nothing is approved that might not merge; an unanswered question is not a yes (F424). The operator can retry once git answers.
requirements.statement: Where the approval gate cannot ask git (a timeout or an OS error), the Hub SHALL refuse the move to `approved` with HTTP 409 and a sentence saying git could not be asked, on every approving surface including landing, rather than answering a server error or approving.

requirements.rationale: Merging a commit merges its ancestors, so the descendant is the whole of the work; recording order alone would let a review of an earlier commit displace newer work.
requirements.statement: Where two accepted footprints name the same line of work, approval SHALL integrate the one whose commit contains the other, else the later recorded; footprints naming no line of work SHALL each be integrated unless another contains them, with a shared commit integrated once and an undecidable pair both integrated.

requirements.rationale: The reviewer has judged the work the evidence demonstrates; a second decision by someone else is what stalled Terra.
requirements.statement: When a task moves to approved, every piece of evidence recorded for that task that is still awaiting MUST be accepted by the approving actor in the same transaction, its review reason being the verdict's notes or, without notes, a sentence naming the approval, except a piece the approving agent recorded itself or whose recording run is still live.
When the approval is refused for any reason, no acceptance made for it MUST persist, and the refusal MUST name the real reason rather than the evidence it would have accepted.

An approval MUST NOT be held for the operator, and a review briefing MUST NOT tell the reviewer that deciding evidence is the operator's, because of evidence recorded for the task under review; the briefing MUST say that the verdict decides that evidence.

requirements.rationale: The operator leaves the gate but keeps the last word.
requirements.statement: When the operator rejects an accepted piece of evidence whose task is approved, the task MUST move to revision_needed with the operator as actor.

requirements.rationale: F681: Land approved a task on evidence another, task-less run recorded at main's tip and skipped the merge, so the task's own commit never reached main while its requirement read verified.
requirements.statement: The Hub SHALL refuse a move to approved, by PATCH and by Land, when the task's own branch holds commits on neither the main branch nor inside any merge target (gate category unlanded), naming the branch and the commits and saying what clears it: evidence recorded from the task's own checkout, then accepted.

A reviewer sending a task back can name the pieces of evidence that fail, each with its own reason, in the same action that sends it back; only the named pieces become rejected, each with its own reason.

requirements.rationale: A piece that held is not wrong; calling it rejected is what made the record and the counts misleading.
requirements.statement: On a send-back, every awaiting piece of the task that the reviewer did not name as failing becomes held at its commit: not rejected, not accepted, and shown as held with the send-back's reason.
A send-back that names no failing piece is allowed when it gives a reason (a defect outside any requirement, a failing check), and then every awaiting piece is held.

requirements.rationale: Operator, 2026-10-26, option B: re-recording is correct by construction; carrying forward waits for slice H's numbers.
requirements.statement: A held piece never counts as accepted evidence; the requirement it served needs a new piece at the builder's next commit, and the reviewer's next verdict judges that new piece.

requirements.rationale: F672: a second decision by someone else stalled finished work.
requirements.statement: Neither the reviewer nor anyone else needs a separate evidence decision before or after the verdict: the send-back or approval decides every awaiting piece of the task in the one action.
Approving a task while naming any of its pieces as failing is refused, naming the contradiction.

list_evidence, the task's history and the app's evidence views show each piece's outcome (accepted, rejected, held, awaiting) with its own reason and who decided it, and filtering by review state distinguishes held from rejected.
The review turn's brief and the update_task tool's description tell the reviewer how to name failing pieces and that unnamed ones are held, not rejected.

requirements.rationale: The command runs with the project's files at landing; like checks, only the operator decides what runs there.
requirements.statement: The operator can set, per project, one or more generated-path globs, the command that rebuilds them, and its timeout, through the same settings route and screen as the project's checks; no agent tool or agent route accepts or changes this setting.
With no generated paths set, every conflict at every conflict point sends the task back exactly as it does today.

When a task's work conflicts with the main branch (or a build's PR branch) only in paths matching the declared globs, at the check run before review, the landing batch or the push to a build's PR, the Hub does not send the task back: it merges the work, runs the command on the merged tree, and continues with the result.
When any conflicting path is outside the declared globs, the task is sent back as merge-needed exactly as today, and the command is not run.

requirements.rationale: The Hub writes this commit without review, so it may contain only files nobody writes by hand.
requirements.statement: A rebuild's result is committed only when the command exits zero within its timeout and every path it changed or created matches a declared glob; otherwise nothing is committed and the task is sent back as merge-needed with a report naming the unexpected paths, the exit code and output tail, or the timeout.
The tree that lands after a rebuild goes through the same checks any landing does; a rebuild never skips or reuses a check result from a different tree.
The command runs in a scratch worktree, never in the project's own checkout, with the Hub's own configuration withheld, the same way a project check runs.

Every rebuild is visible afterwards: the merge commit message says generated files were rebuilt, and the landing or check-run record and the task's history name the rebuilt paths and how long the command took.

requirements.rationale: 2026-10-27: QA's approval of T1 was refused for 2 h 40 min while checks ran and re-ran. The landing check is the batch's run on the real merged result (one-check-run-per-batch), so making approval wait for a current per-task result only repeats it.
requirements.statement: In a project with checks configured, a move to approved that is refused for no other reason is recorded at once and queues the task's work for landing. It is not refused because the task's check result is missing, still running, or was produced on an earlier main tip. Approving starts no per-task check run. Approval is still refused when the task's own confirmed check failure is recorded for the same merge targets.

requirements.rationale: Ten full-suite runs of 8-18 min on 2026-10-26/27, most of them re-runs because another landing had moved main.
requirements.statement: Tasks queued for landing in one project are landed together in a batch. Main's tip, with every batch task's merge targets merged in queue order, gets one run of the project's checks. When that run passes, every task in the batch reaches main and no further check run is started for any of them.

After a batch lands, the tree at main's tip equals the tree the batch's checks passed on, and each landed task has one merged integration record per merge target, with the commits that rode along. If main's tip moved after the batch was built, nothing lands from the stale batch, and the batch is built and checked again on the new tip.

requirements.rationale: The roadmap's done criterion: a deliberately broken task among four is the only one sent back.
requirements.statement: When a batch's checks fail with a confirmed failure that is not main's, the Hub finds the first task in queue order whose work, added to the tasks before it, makes the failing tests fail. Only that task goes back to its author (approved to revision_needed), with the failing output and the tasks it was landed on. The rest of the batch is checked again as the next batch and lands if it passes. Finding the task takes at most ceil(log2(n)) narrowed runs for a batch of n, and each narrowed run executes only the failed tests when the check is a plain pytest command.

requirements.rationale: Reconciling two pieces of work is the later author's job, as for a conflicting prerequisite (`a-conflicting-prerequisite-is-the-authors-to-merge`).
requirements.statement: A queued task whose work does not merge cleanly onto main plus the batch tasks before it is taken out of the batch before any check runs. It is sent back to its author naming the conflicting paths and the tasks it conflicts with, and the rest of the batch proceeds without it.

requirements.rationale: A merge brings in a commit's whole ancestry (F58, `task_integration.py:727-729`). A dependent landing first would put its prerequisite's unchecked or sent-back work on main under the dependent's name.
requirements.statement: A queued task lands only in a batch where every task whose commit its merge targets contain has already landed or comes earlier in the same batch. If such a prerequisite is sent back, the dependent stays queued, is not sent back, and its landing names the prerequisite it waits for.

requirements.rationale: Today the merge (up to 2.1 s), the release (p95 10.3 s) and any mutation-lock wait (up to 20.8 s) run after the approval's first write and before its commit, so every other writer waits (F349 is the same shape on another route).
requirements.statement: No approval, landing, integration retry, mend resolution or checkout release holds a database write transaction open while a git command or a check runs. A write from another database connection made while that git runs completes without waiting for it.

requirements.rationale: Under slice L the per-task run gives the builder fast feedback and gates review. Landing safety comes from the batch's run on the merged result, so re-running every waiting task on each landing is spent work.
requirements.statement: When main's tip moves, the Hub does not re-run the checks of a task waiting for review whose latest per-task result passed. That result counts as passed for review dispatch and for approval whatever tip it was produced on. A task with no result, an interrupted result or an errored result still gets a run.

requirements.rationale: Slice B made a check wait visible beside Land (FR a-wait-is-visible). The wait now belongs to the batch, so that is what the drawer shows.
requirements.statement: The task's drawer and its checks route show its landing state: queued (with its position), checking (with the batch, how long it has run and how long the previous batch took), held (and on what), landed (with the commit), or sent back (with the failing check's output). The operator is notified when a batch lands or sends a task back, without reloading.

requirements.rationale: One writer keeps a batch's base from moving under it, so every landing is checked, and the 24 hub test files that assert an integration outcome after approval keep their meaning in projects without checks.
requirements.statement: Every merge the Hub makes into main goes through the landing queue, at most one batch at a time per project. That covers approval, retrying an integration, landing a mend resolution, and integrating approved work whose evidence was accepted afterwards. With no checks configured, the landing still runs after the approval commits, and the request that caused it answers with the integration outcome as it does today. With checks configured, the request answers at once with the task queued.

requirements.rationale: The operator's :8000 runs this checkout and is restarted by the operator, sometimes mid-flow.
requirements.statement: If the Hub stops while a batch is being checked or landed, then after it starts again no queued task is lost and none is merged twice. A batch left checking is recorded interrupted and its tasks are queued again in their original order. A batch that had already moved main is recorded landed from what main contains.

in_scope: Merging approved work into the configured main branch, locally, in the approval transition
Choosing the commit: accepted evidence footprints reduced per line of work, other tasks' evidence once they are approved, or the task branch tip where evidence does not govern
Approval refusals about what would merge: conflicts, a live turn still producing the work, unaccepted evidence, git unavailable
Recording every attempt (merged, skipped, failed), work already in the main line, and retryability
Re-attempting integration on retry, on naming the main branch, and on accepting evidence
non_goals: The task status machine, actor separation and field ownership: task-lifecycle-governance
Running project checks and the check gate with its operator override: project-checks
Setting and detecting the project's main branch: local-project-workspace
Recording and reviewing evidence, and coverage: requirement-traceability
Releasing a finished task's checkout: workspace-isolation

summary: What approving a task does to the code. Approval merges the approved work into the project's main branch in the same operation, choosing which commit to merge; it is refused when that merge would conflict, when the work is still being produced, when evidence that would merge is unaccepted, or when git cannot be asked. Every integration attempt is recorded, a skipped one can be retried, and a preview says what approval would merge.
title: Approval integration
